Neonates of the Short-headed lamprey emerge from the gravel nest as ammocoetes, and at this earliest life stage the wet weight at birth is a mere 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams]. These larval individuals remain burrowed in the sediment for several years, feeding on detritus and algae, before undergoing a dramatic metamorphosis that transforms them into the parasitic adult phase. The transition to the parasitic stage is accompanied by the development of a functional oral disc and eyes, and it is within this period that individuals begin their rapid somatic growth. Field records indicate that following the onset of active feeding on host fish, the lampreys attain an ultimate total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a dimension that represents the maximum size observed in the wild. This length is consistent with the body size reported for other members of the Mordaciidae but notably smaller than the giant lampreys of the Northern Hemisphere.

Reproductive maturation in Mordacia mordax is a clearly defined event linked to body size rather than strict chronological age. The total length at puberty has been determined to be 11.3 centimeters [Lp = 11.3 centimeters], a threshold that must be reached before the onset of gonadal development and downstream spawning migration. At this pubertal size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 1.73 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.73 grams], a mass that reflects the energetic reserves necessary for the fasting migratory phase that precedes reproduction. This relationship between length and mass is close to that predicted by a simple cubic scaling relationship typical of many vertebrate species. Individuals that have not yet attained this size remain in a pre-reproductive juvenile state, continuing their parasitic feeding until the appropriate body dimensions are realized. The timing of this event is variable and heavily influenced by host availability, water temperature, and the individual's success in acquiring somatic resources during the parasitic phase.

Fecundity in this species is a terminal event, as adults spawn once and then die, a life cycle characteristic of many lampreys. The total number of eggs produced at the end of life, measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], has been recorded as 13,372 eggs . This reproductive output is deposited in a single spawning event within gravel nests in freshwater streams, after which both males and females succumb to physiological exhaustion. The eggs are small, with a mean diameter of about one millimeter, indicating a strategy of producing a large number of relatively tiny offspring rather than a small number of well-provisioned ones. Such a high fecundity is typical of semelparous species where parental care is absent and offspring survival is low. The dependence on fine gravel substrates for successful egg incubation makes the species particularly sensitive to habitat degradation and siltation.

The life span of Mordacia mordax is remarkably short for a fish that undergoes such a dramatic metamorphosis, and it is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of its natal stream. At a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the maximum life span has been estimated at 9 years [am = 9 years], encompassing the extended larval phase of several years, the relatively brief parasitic feeding stage, and the final spawning migration. This total longevity is a composite of the variable-length ammocoete period, which can range from three to five years depending on local productivity and temperature, followed by a parasitic phase of approximately one to two years, and culminating in the non-feeding reproductive migration that lasts only a few months. The thermal dependency of this life span is pronounced; cooler stream temperatures can extend the larval period considerably, while warmer conditions accelerate development but may reduce overall longevity. This trade-off between temperature, growth rate, and lifespan is a critical component of the species' life-history strategy in the face of changing climate conditions.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by a fully grown adult of this species is approximately 150 grams [Wwi = approximately 150 grams], a mass that represents the maximum potential body size attained at the end of the parasitic feeding phase before the onset of the spawning migration. This body mass stands in stark contrast to the minute size of the larval form at hatching, which weighs only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], illustrating a dramatic growth trajectory spanning several orders of magnitude. The allometric relationship between length and weight in Mordacia mordax follows a cubic scaling, such that the 50 centimeter [Li = 50 centimeter] ultimate length yields a predicted weight of 150 grams based on the species-specific condition factor. This condition factor is similar to that reported for other parasitic lampreys, reflecting a relatively slender body shape typical of the group. Such a high adult-to-neonate mass ratio necessitates an efficient feeding mechanism and a rich supply of host blood, which the adults exploit during their parasitic phase.
